title: Are We Becoming Grumbles?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by re-reading an old article from his archives, Dave Stuart Jr. revisits the danger of habitual complaining in teaching, opening with a memory of a veteran teaching couple whose relentless complaining seemed to be corroding both their performance and their character. He walks through and dismantles the common rationalizations teachers give for complaining — that it's therapeutic, that venting is important, that it builds camaraderie — arguing these are unexamined statements of faith rather than defensible claims. He then builds the case against complaining in stages: it wastes time because it produces nothing of value, it warps the complainer's inner state toward either powerlessness or pride, and left unchecked it can become part of a person's identity rather than just a habit. Stuart leans on C. S. Lewis's The Great Divorce to dramatize the endpoint of this trajectory, where a soul can become indistinguishable from its own grumbling. He closes by acknowledging his own tendency to complain and inviting readers to interrogate their justifications while remembering that persistent complaining, unlike much else in teaching, is fully within a teacher's control.
points: Common justifications for complaining (it's therapeutic, it's venting, it builds camaraderie) function as unexamined statements of faith that collapse under simple scrutiny — Stuart notes even Hitler and the KKK had strong camaraderie, so community alone can't justify a habit.

Complaining has a compounding cost structure: first it wastes the time spent complaining, then it warps the complainer's internal state toward powerlessness or pride, draining productivity and focus beyond the complaining session itself.

C. S. Lewis's distinction between 'a grumbler' and 'only a grumble' in The Great Divorce illustrates how habitual complaint can eventually consume the complainer's identity, leaving no self left to critique the habit.
Complaining shows up twice as costly for teachers specifically, since it both fails to solve the problem being complained about and erodes the complainer's capacity to do their best work afterward.
Stuart frames complaining as one of the few things fully within a teacher's control, even amid the many things about the job that genuinely aren't controllable.
quotes: I'm not talking about the solutions-oriented, disciplined discussion of problems; I'm talking about relentless, incorrigible problem-pointing-out.

Do we have proof that there is therapeutic value in a habit of complaining? Does any school of psychology uphold this? Shall we do all things that make us feel better? Cocaine can make you feel better, I've heard. So can cigarettes. And Oreos.

So at best, complaining wastes the time it takes to complain. Unfortunately, complaining wastes more than just the time it takes to complain, because complaining does make something inside of us, and I think what it makes can vary.
The question is whether she is a grumbler, or only a grumble. If there is a real woman — even the least trace of one — still there inside the grumbling, it can be brought to life again.
It just is us; we just are a complaint, something so much less than a person.
There are so many things we can't control, but every teacher in the world can choose whether or not to persist in complaining.
